clue.text: Top model every year ran out of energy

parts.note: PA is short for per annum, Latin for each year

indicators.note: out here means disordered, so the letters of ran and GO are rearranged

parts.note: go means energy or vigour, as in 'full of go'

explanation.surface: A leading fashion model, worn out after a year of shows, loses her energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' is the anagram signal for ran plus the energy word. 'Top model' reads as a catwalk star but is a model in the sense of a perfect example.
explanation.definitionFit: An exemplar of perfection is a model to imitate, and 'top' stresses the very best such example.

clue.text: Fleece attendant the Spanish brought in

indicators.note: brought in means introduced within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a page is a young attendant
el is the Spanish masculine article meaning the

explanation.surface: A servant's fleecy coat that the Spanish introduced.
explanation.definitionFit: This zoological term means an animal's coat of fur, hair or wool, such as a sheep's wool.

clue.text: Disturb fellow and female breaking the law

indicators.note: breaking means splitting open, so the two letters break into the law word

parts.note: a rule is a law or regulation
F is an abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS

explanation.surface: A man and a woman cause disturbance by breaking the law.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsettle or agitate someone is to ruffle their feathers, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Water pipe goes wonky, swamping forest hotel

indicators.note: swamping means engulfing, so the rearranged letters surround the forest and hotel
wonky means askew or crooked, so the letters of goes are rearranged

parts.note: the Forest of Arden is the setting of As You Like It
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A water pipe has burst, flooding a woodland hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wonky' rearranges goes as GOSE, and 'swamping' wraps that round forest and hotel. Arden is the forest of Shakespeare's As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: A flexible tube for watering plants is a kind of water pipe.

clue.text: Collar on old boy's top dog

indicators.note: on means placed before in a down clue, so the collar word sits above the old boy

parts.note: to collar is to nab or arrest
OB is the abbreviation for old boy; the 's means 'is', linking to the definition

explanation.surface: Putting a collar on the old boy's top dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A wealthy, important person, originally a nobleman in Mughal India, is a big shot or top dog.

clue.text: Extremely pretty stuff like dark clothing?

indicators.note: extremely points to the extreme letters, the first and last, of pretty

parts.note: to stuff is to cram, as to jam
as means like, in the sense of similar to

explanation.surface: A fashion note about very pretty material resembling something dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dark clothing' is clothing for the dark, i.e. for night-time, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightwear is worn after dark, so it can be whimsically called clothing for the dark.

clue.text: Film dog and feline running round royal 4

definitions.note: a cross-reference to the answer at 4-down, a rich and powerful person

parts.note: Pluto is Mickey Mouse's dog in Disney cartoons

indicators.note: running round means encircling, so the feline word goes round the royal letter

parts.note: a cat is a feline
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: A cartoon dog and a cat chase each other around a royal person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone whose power comes from great wealth, a rich bigwig.

clue.text: Yank's jack and king capturing queen

indicators.note: capturing means taking prisoner, so the queen letters are held between jack and king

parts.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack
K is the card abbreviation for king
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the queen

explanation.surface: An American's card hand: jack and king taking the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank's' tempts towards an American; it is the verb yank, with 's meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden sharp pull is a tug, so to yank something is to give it a sharp tug.

clue.text: Rule operating during parade at end of May

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so the operating word sits inside the parade word

parts.note: a march is a parade or procession
on means operating, as a switched-on machine

indicators.note: at end of takes the final letter of May

explanation.surface: A rule operating during a May Day parade.
explanation.definitionFit: Government by a king or queen is a form of rule, and a monarch's reign.

clue.text: Cornish consumers are the tops

parts.note: Cornwall is in the south-west of England, abbreviated SW
eaters are consumers of food

explanation.surface: People in Cornwall who eat are the best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the tops' looks like praise meaning 'the best', but tops are garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumpers and pullovers are knitted garments worn on the upper body, which are called tops.

clue.text: Current judge retires after initially libelling prisoner

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of libelling

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current

indicators.note: retires means goes back, so the word for judge is read backwards

parts.note: a ref, or referee, judges a game

explanation.surface: A sitting judge steps down after a libel case involving an inmate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retires' means goes back, so the judge is read backwards; 'after' places the libelling letter first.
explanation.definitionFit: A convict serving a life sentence is a long-term prisoner, so the slang term fits.

clue.text: Typically rich female Conservative rebel defends name

parts.note: blue is the colour of the UK Conservative Party

indicators.note: defends means surrounds protectively, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: to rise is to rebel, as in a rising against rulers

explanation.surface: A wealthy Tory woman turns rebel but sticks up for someone's name.
explanation.walkthrough: A blue rinse is a bluish hair tint associated with well-off older women, so the term stands for such a woman, hence 'Typically'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bluish hair tint became shorthand for prosperous elderly ladies, so it can label a typical wealthy woman.

clue.text: Unusually bold one got football award

indicators.note: unusually signals the letters of bold, one and got are arranged in an unusual order

explanation.surface: An unusually daring player won a football prize.
explanation.definitionFit: The trophy is presented to a league or tournament's top goalscorer in football.

clue.text: Now and then turn out for brisk walk

indicators.note: now and then means occasionally, so only every other letter of turn out is taken

explanation.surface: Every so often, someone goes out for a quick stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick jogging pace, between walking and running, is what this word denotes.

clue.text: Shock! Bouquets given to setters!

parts.note: a shock of hair is a thick mass of it, so shock stands for hair
sprays are bunches of flowers

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise as flowers are presented to crossword setters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setters' looks like crossword compilers, but here means products that set a hairstyle.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacquers sprayed on to hold a hairstyle in place are hair setting products.

clue.text: She had bra fixed by top woman dealer for buttons

indicators.note: fixed means rearranged or adjusted, so the letters of she had bra are reordered

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen, the top woman

explanation.surface: A woman adjusts her bra with help from a senior female shop worker selling buttons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fixed' rearranges SHE HAD BRA into HABERDASH, then ER is added; 'by' simply places it beside.
explanation.definitionFit: A haberdasher's shop sells sewing notions such as thread, ribbons and buttons.

clue.text: Potty's not supported at the top in lodging

indicators.note: lodging means staying within, so in sits inside the other piece

parts.note: a woman not supported at the top is without a bra

explanation.surface: A daft remark about someone going without support in a guest house.
explanation.definitionFit: Potty is British slang for foolish or crazy, which describes someone lacking brains.

clue.text: Society which admits inexperienced boater for one

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so raw goes inside that

parts.note: that can mean which, as a relative pronoun
a raw recruit is inexperienced

explanation.surface: A rowing club that lets in a novice rower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boater' suggests someone in a boat, but it is the flat-topped hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A boater is a stiff flat-brimmed hat of plaited fibre, so it is one example.

clue.text: A doctor regularly pulls soldier fit to walk

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at regular intervals from pulls

parts.note: a soldier ant is a classic crossword soldier

explanation.surface: A doctor regularly checks a soldier is fit for marching.
explanation.definitionFit: This adjective describes a patient able to walk about rather than being bedridden.

clue.text: Burns lines, 25

definitions.meaning: a narrative poem by Robert Burns, the Scottish poet, about a farmer chased by witches
a cross-reference to the answer at 25-across, top gear, here a Scottish bonnet named after that poem's hero

explanation.surface: A cryptic pairing of a poet's verse and another clue's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet; his poem about a farmer's ride gave its name to the woollen Scots bonnet.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's title character lent his name to the round woollen cap worn in Scotland, a type of hat.

clue.text: Nice one to choose to extract sewer's product?

parts.note: un is French for one, as spoken in Nice
to pick is to choose

explanation.surface: A French person deciding how to empty a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewer' reads as a drain, but it is someone who sews; 'Nice' is the French city, not a compliment.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo stitching is to take out the work of someone who sews, hence removing a seamstress's product.

clue.text: Repair this initially rather tempting top

indicators.note: repair means mend or reassemble, so the letters of this are rearranged
initially takes the first letters of rather and tempting

explanation.surface: A tempting top that needs mending.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual collarless cotton shirt with short sleeves is a top worn on the upper body.

clue.text: March on a reservation

parts.note: a but is a reservation or objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'

explanation.surface: Soldiers march on to a native reservation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' is not walking: a march is a border, so to march on is to share a boundary with.
explanation.definitionFit: Marches are borderlands, so to march on something is to border it or lie adjacent.

clue.text: Bits covered by these foreign articles? Rubbish!

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article and der the German definite article, together two foreign articles
pants is British slang for rubbish or nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses foreign articles of clothing as rubbish, wondering what bits they cover.
explanation.walkthrough: One clue phrase gives two articles, UN (French) and DER (German); 'pants' as British slang for rubbish completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Knickers and briefs cover the private parts, the bits referred to coyly in the clue.

clue.text: Record a few short races here

parts.note: an EP, extended play, is a type of record

indicators.note: short means cut off at the end, so the final letter of the word for a few is dropped

parts.note: some means a few

explanation.surface: Recording a handful of brief races.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom is the Surrey racecourse where the Derby is run.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse races are held at this English racecourse, home of the Derby.

clue.text: Move carefully, say, touring Germany and Spain

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the example word goes round the letter for Germany

parts.note: eg, for example, is signalled by say
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: Driving cautiously on a tour of Germany and Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch forward cautiously is to edge along, a verb of slow careful movement.

clue.text: Ambassador has to deal with Top Gear

parts.note: HE stands for His Excellency, the title of an ambassador
to address a problem is to deal with it

explanation.surface: An ambassador has to tackle the Top Gear motoring programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Top Gear is a famous BBC motoring show, but here it means gear worn on top, on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Headgear such as a hat or crown is worn on top of the head, hence top gear.

clue.text: Excuse one in vestment beside the writer

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the letter for one goes within the vestment

parts.note: an alb is a white ecclesiastical vestment
I is the Roman numeral for one
the writer refers to the setter, who would say I

explanation.surface: A priest excuses a man in robes standing beside the author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beside' places the writer's I after ALIB.
explanation.definitionFit: A claim of being elsewhere at the time of a crime serves as a defence or pretext.

clue.text: At first, trouble and strife shattered tiles

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of trouble
shattered means broken into pieces, so the letters of strife are rearranged

explanation.surface: A roofer's lament: at first, trouble and strife shattered the tiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble and strife' is cockney rhyming slang for wife, a decoy here. 'shattered' turns STRIFE into ITFERS. Titfer (from tit-for-tat, rhyming with hat) and tile are both British slang for hats.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are British slang for hats, one from cockney rhyming slang.

clue.text: City police seizing second runner's formal wear

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold of, so the police word wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police
a ski is a runner on snow; the 's joins it to the definition

explanation.surface: London police arrest an athlete in a hurry, still in evening dress.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the formal evening uniform worn by military officers at dinners in the officers' mess.
